definition: PSOLA (Pitch Synchronous Overlap and Add) is a digital signal processing technique used for speech processing and more specifically speech synthesis.
details: It can be used to modify the pitch and duration of a speech signal. It was invented around 1986. PSOLA works by dividing the speech waveform in small overlapping segments. To change the pitch of the signal, the segments are moved further apart (to decrease the pitch) or closer together (to increase the pitch). To change the duration of the signal, the segments are then repeated multiple times (to increase the duration) or some are eliminated (to decrease the duration). The segments are then combined using the overlap add technique. PSOLA can be used to change the prosody of a speech signal.

explainer.lead: PSOLA modifies the pitch and duration of speech signals by manipulating overlapping waveform segments, which makes it useful for speech synthesis.

tiers.eli5: It chops the voice recording into small overlapping pieces and slides or repeats them to make the voice higher, lower, longer, or shorter.
tiers.practitioner: It is used in speech synthesis to retime and repitch recorded speech; a pitfall is that moving segments too far apart or dropping too many can introduce audible artefacts.
tiers.paperLevel: Invented around 1986, it divides the speech waveform into small overlapping segments, moves them closer or further apart to change pitch, and repeats or removes them to change duration before recombining.

explainer.example: To raise the pitch of a recorded word, its segments are spaced closer together, then recombined into the output waveform.
